content:
Being a single cat lady has never felt more appealing.

Comedian Shane Gillis is the subject of a haunting new essay in The Cut written by his ex-girlfriend Grace Brassel — and it reads like a cautionary tale.

“What I’ve learned is that while my experience may seem exceptional because it involved private jet rides and hanging out with celebrities, how Shane made me feel could not be more textbook,” Brassel wrote in her essay. “Men like him exist in every tax bracket. They put you on a pedestal, kick it out from under you, and tell you it was your fault you fell.”

Brassel began her essay by acknowledging the elephant in the room: Gillis’ self-described “C-minus of a monologue” for “Saturday Night Live” in October, when he notoriously said that women at the gym nowadays dress like “whores.”

“I wasn’t the least bit surprised,” she wrote of the joke. “After our time together, how do I think he feels about women? He doesn’t like them much.”

But at least the moment provided Brassel with some “closure,” she said, because “people were finally seeing the man I knew.”

Echoing his statement to The Cut, Gillis told HuffPost: “Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best.”

Brassel wrote that she dated Gillis for a little over a year — from May 2024 to August 2025. Gillis was well into his 30s at the time, and Brassel was a 25-year-old living in New Jersey, working a marketing job and growing a following on TikTok. She wrote that she was instantly attracted to Gillis after a friend introduced her to his Netflix series “Tires,” and she decided to slide into his DMs.

“‘Hey, if you’re ever in New York, let’s go on an adventure,’ I wrote to him, not expecting anything,” Brassel wrote. “He replied alarmingly fast, telling me to give him my phone number. My roommate and I were jumping up and down in our tiny apartment. The guy from the TV wanted my number!”

The two began chatting, and Gillis offered to fly Brassel out to Austin, Texas, to meet. Gillis got her a room at the Four Seasons, and they engaged in a weekend she described as “a dream” in which Gillis said “all the right things.”

“He thought I was beautiful and treated me with care,” Brassel wrote, adding: “By the time I left Austin, we were official.”

Two months later, they moved into a house in Philadelphia together.

“Once we started living together, it was a nonstop party — Eagles games, long nights of drinking, hanging out with celebrities. Wash, rinse, repeat,” Brassel wrote. “It became harder and harder to work my day job as a social-media manager, so Shane told me I should just quit.”

She added: “Little did I know I had actually just accepted a different full-time position, one that had a high rate of burnout and no chance for upward mobility: Shane Gillis’s stay-at-home girlfriend.”

Brassel wrote that being Gillis’ “25-year-old housewife” wasn’t too bad at first, despite his “frat boy” lifestyle that “had no structure.”

Things took a turn, however, when the couple decided to move to West Chester, Pennsylvania, and Gillis suddenly expected Brassel to be “someone who cooked, cleaned, did the laundry, and waited for her man to come home from a long day at work.”

“When things weren’t exactly to his liking, he would tell me that I wasn’t ‘being good.’ You know, the way you would talk to a dog,” she wrote.

She also began to notice a more sinister side of the seemingly happy-go-lucky comedian.

“Shane would often say something remarkably cruel and then play it off like a joke,” Brassel wrote. “He did it with me, he does it with his friends, and I saw him do it with his colleagues.”

And there were other “red flags,” Brassel said, including that he’d refer to women as “whores” and began policing what she could wear, including her Halloween costume at a party he’d tasked her with throwing.

Brassel began to spiral under the stress. Her friends — who were all out of state — began to get concerned and “jokingly asked if I was experiencing psychosis.” She said that at this point, she “cried every day.”

Things got even worse when the couple decided to move to Austin, according to Brassel. Gillis became even more distant, and she was even farther from her support system. He scored Super Bowl tickets and didn’t invite her along. He hosted “SNL” on her birthday, and when Brassel asked about celebrating, he told her she was “lucky I’m even fucking inviting you to this,” according to Brassel.

Things came to a head on July Fourth, Brassel said, when she used Gillis’ phone to play music and discovered he was cheating on her, spelling the end of their relationship.

Brassel said Gillis’ fans harassed her for months after they broke up — and that one even physically assaulted her.

Eventually, she turned to therapy and had a revelation.

“I spent so much time trying to understand what happened only to realize the answer is actually kind of boring,” Brassel wrote. “Guys like that are insecure, and instead of choosing to be better men, they take their shortcomings out on everyone else around them.”

Read Brassel’s full essay — which includes some very weird details about Joe Rogan and an O.J. Simpson estate sale — over at The Cut.
